title: Right seats, right sheet music
allegory: Building ResNet34 and loading pretrained weights is like seating an orchestra on chairs you built yourself, then handing out a famous orchestra's sheet music in seat order: if every chair is in the right place, it plays the same song as the original.
map: BlockGroups, each a run of residual blocks at one width
the chairs you place, in the order you place them
the famous orchestra's sheet music, one folder per chair
torchvision's pretrained tensors, one per state_dict entry
handing out folders by seat number, never reading names
copy_weights zipping the two state_dicts' keys by position
playing the same piece and listening side by side
running both models on the same images and comparing the argmax

chapters.name: Deeper got worse
chapters.note: worse on data it has already seen?

cap.1: Researchers stacked a network 56 layers deep and it did worse than a 20-layer one, even on data it had already seen. More layers made it harder to train.
cap.2: He, Zhang, Ren and Sun found a 56-layer plain net had higher training error than a 20-layer one on CIFAR-10. Not overfitting: it could not even fit. Residual blocks fixed it.
cap.3: The degradation problem: extra layers could be identity, so this is optimisation failure, not capacity. The residual fix reached 152 layers, 3.57% ImageNet error, ILSVRC 2015 first place.

cap.1: Each block hands on what it received plus a small correction. If the best move is to change nothing, the block only has to learn zeros.
cap.2: A ResidualBlock is two 3x3 convs with batchnorm, then the input is added back. The add needs equal shapes, so a downsampling block gets a 1x1 stride-2 conv on its skip.
cap.3: H(x) = F(x) + x makes identity the zero of F and gives gradients an additive path. Where a block downsamples, the identity branch needs a 1x1 stride-2 conv plus BN.

chapters.name: Seat the orchestra
chapters.note: every chair is a module you wrote

cap.1: Picture seating an orchestra on chairs you built yourself: players in sections, sections in a fixed order. That is ResNet34, built from your own modules.
cap.2: ResNet34 stacks BlockGroups, each a run of ResidualBlocks at one width where only the first block may change shape. You build it from your own modules, then check the parameter count.
cap.3: Assemble ResidualBlock, BlockGroup, ResNet34, then check against print_param_count and torchinfo.summary. Module registration order silently fixes the state_dict key order.

cap.1: Now hand out a famous orchestra's sheet music: walk down both seating lists together, first folder to first chair. Nobody reads the names.
cap.2: copy_weights builds your state_dict by zipping your keys against torchvision's tensors in order. It pairs by position, never by name.
cap.3: The copy is a positional zip of two ordered state_dicts, not a name match. Your registration order, including branch order inside blocks, must mirror torchvision's.

chapters.name: One seat off
chapters.verdict: Loading without an error proves nothing. Compare the predictions.

cap.1: Swap two chairs and folders land on the wrong seats. Many parts still fit the stand, so nobody complains. The music is just wrong.
cap.2: ResNet repeats the same kernel and batchnorm shapes, so a misordered copy often loads with no error. The model runs and predicts confident nonsense.
cap.3: Repeated (64,64,3,3) kernels and equal-width BN vectors make misalignment shape-valid. Print the zipped key pairs, match torchinfo.summary, then compare argmax end to end.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Print both key lists side by side

cap.1: Loading without an error proves nothing. Getting the same answers as the original does. You will reuse this check on every model you rebuild.
cap.2: Counts catch missing layers, key pairs catch order, and matching argmax on real images catches the rest. The same recipe validates any reimplementation.
cap.3: When you study a real model inside code you can read and hook, matching the reference outputs is what lets you draw conclusions about that model, not your copy of it.

coda.title: Match each symptom to what went wrong
pairs: A layer is missing or extra
Loads without error, predicts confident nonsense
Modules registered in the wrong order
Can't add x to F(x) in a downsampling block
The skip needs a 1x1 stride-2 conv and batchnorm
Good in training, bad at eval time
A deeper plain net has higher training error
Same argmax as torchvision on the sample images

caption.1: Match each symptom to its cause. The sneaky one is the model that loads fine and still gets everything wrong.
caption.2: Each symptom points at a different check: counts catch missing layers, key pairs catch order, and predictions catch everything else.
caption.3: Arity, ordering, shape and mode errors fail in different ways; only an end-to-end argmax comparison against the reference covers them all at once.

where_else: Porting any model between frameworks: load the original weights, then compare outputs
Interpretability tools that load a real model's weights into code you can read and hook
The transformer residual stream, the same add-it-back structure at the heart of chapter 1
Any refactor: the new code should give the old code's outputs on the same inputs

hamming.what: ResNet34 is residual blocks grouped into BlockGroups, and loading real pretrained weights into your own copy is the test that you built it exactly right.
hamming.when: Whenever you reimplement a known model: match its parameter count first, then its predictions.
hamming.why: A wrong architecture rarely raises an error, so agreeing with a trusted reference is the only proof that you have the same model.

object.title: The seating plan
object.subtitle: Two rows of pegs: the slots your model offers, and the tensors that land in them.

cap.1: Front row: the slot each of your modules offers. Back row: the tensor that gets handed over. Lined up, every peg matches.
cap.2: Tall pegs are conv kernels, short ones batchnorm vectors. Height also creeps up a little per layer, so each tensor is unique.
cap.3: Big height = shape class; the small per-layer increment = tensor identity. With shift 0 the positional zip pairs every key correctly.

cap.1: Shift by one: a tall kernel lands in a short batchnorm slot. This mistake is loud. Loading fails straight away.
cap.2: Off by one, shapes clash and load_state_dict raises a size mismatch. Annoying, but at least you are told.
cap.3: A misalignment that breaks shape agreement is caught by load_state_dict; these are the cheap bugs.

cap.1: Shift by a whole layer: every tall peg lands on a tall slot again. No error at all. Yet each one came from the wrong layer.
cap.2: Shift by one repeating unit and every shape matches again. Loading succeeds silently with every tensor in the wrong place.
cap.3: Because ResNet repeats identical shapes, a shift by one period is shape-valid: the failure mode no size check can see.

cap.1: That small height difference is the whole bug: right shape, wrong tensor. Only comparing answers with the original catches it.
cap.2: Look at the small steps between rows. Printing zipped key pairs shows this at once; comparing argmax proves the fix.
cap.3: Identity mismatch under shape agreement is detectable only by name diffing the zipped keys or by end-to-end output comparison.

cap.1: Back in order. Now your model gives the same predictions as the original, which is the real test.
cap.2: The fix: register modules in torchvision's order, check counts, print pairs, and compare predictions on the sample images.
cap.3: Once order mirrors the reference, predictions match; the same end-to-end check validates any reimplementation, framework port or hooked model copy.

predict.q: copy_weights ran and load_state_dict raised nothing. Is your ResNet34 right?

options.t: Not necessarily: same-shaped tensors can land in the wrong slots
Yes: any mistake would raise a shape error

predict.why: ResNet repeats the same kernel and batchnorm shapes, so a misordered copy can be perfectly shape-valid.

predict.q: Which check covers ordering, shapes and buffers all at once?

options.t: Running both models on the same images and comparing the argmax

predict.why: The count catches missing or extra layers. Only matching predictions proves everything lines up.

predict.q: When a block downsamples, why does its skip path need a 1x1 conv?

options.t: The stride-2 downsample changes the shape, so x cannot be added to F(x) as it is
To give the block more parameters

predict.why: The addition needs matching shapes. The 1x1 stride-2 conv plus batchnorm reshapes the skip to fit.

object.where: Any rebuild checked against a reference: framework ports, refactors, hooked copies of real models.
